title: The prince with no equal
hookLine: Satyavati's proud son thinks no one is his equal, and Hindu teaching has a name for that
carry: ahamkara: the ego that says no equal

cards: Two warriors face each other, and they share a name. One is a prince of the Kurus. The other is a powerful king of the Gandharvas, the heavenly musicians.

The text calls them namesakes, and says the Gandharva came looking for this fight. That's how the story of Satyavati's first son ends. To get there, go back to the palace, where the fisherman's daughter is now a queen.

teach.h: A PROUD SON ON THE THRONE.
teach.b: Satyavati has married King Shantanu on the terms Bhishma's vow made possible. She bears him two sons, Chitrangada and then Vichitravirya. Before the younger is grown, Shantanu dies.

Bhishma keeps his word: he places Chitrangada on the throne and answers to Satyavati as his mother. Chitrangada is strong, and the text says he's proud. He defeats king after king, and comes to think no one is his equal.
That's when the Gandharva of the same name arrives, looking for this fight.

They fight at Kurukshetra, beside the Sarasvati, long and hard, and the Gandharva, with the illusions of his kind, kills the prince. Bhishma performs the funeral rites, and sets the boy Vichitravirya on the throne.
The poem gives Satyavati no speech; her grief stays quiet. Now the teaching.
Hindu thought has a name for what grew in Chitrangada: ahamkara, literally the I-maker. It's the voice that says, I did this, I'm the best, no one's my equal.

The Bhagavad Gita, spoken later on this same field of Kurukshetra, says the one deluded by ahamkara thinks, I am the doer, when it's nature doing the work, and it lists pride and arrogance among the marks of a demonic nature.
It isn't a rule against being good at things. Chitrangada really did win. The trouble was the story he told himself about it.
That's why many Hindus end a puja by offering it back, some saying Krishnarpanam, given to Krishna, and why touching an elder's feet is a small, daily bow of the I.

how: Many Hindus end a puja by offering the worship and its fruits back to God, some with the words 'Krishnarpanam astu', may it be an offering to Krishna; touching an elder's feet is another everyday bow of the ego.

s: the Gita says it's wrong to be good at things
it warns about ahamkara, the 'i alone did it' story, not about skill.
Bhishma took the throne when Shantanu died
he kept his vow and placed Chitrangada on it.
the fight took place at Kurukshetra
by the Sarasvati: the same field where Krishna will speak the Gita.

games.q: after the puja, Nani holds your report card up and says 'Krishnarpanam'. what's she doing?
o: offering the success back to God, so ahamkara doesn't take all the credit.
asking God for a better grade next term.
blessing the paper so it won't get lost.
games.why: Chitrangada kept every win for himself until no one was his equal. offering a success back is the Hindu habit that keeps the I-maker small.

practice: Think of one thing you did well lately. Hold it and enjoy it; that's allowed. Then, the way many Hindus close a prayer, set it down: fold your hands and bow your head.
If you pray, offer it to God, in your own words. If you don't, thank the people, the teachers and the luck that helped. Notice that the win is still yours, and lighter.

wordCard.voice: Satyavati. A widowed queen with one son lost to his own pride and his namesake, and one boy left on the throne.

orig.note: Sanskrit ahaṃkāra, the I-maker: the ego that says 'I am the doer', as the Gita puts it.

carryVoice: Your line: ahamkara, the ego that says no equal. A boy king, a queen mother and a vow now hold the house. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Adi Parva, Sambhava Parva (the sons of Satyavati; Shantanu's death; Chitrangada slain by the Gandharva Chitrangada; Vichitravirya installed)
